before: Before choosing any tool for a piece of writing, each student describes in their own words what is actually hard about it for them. They are specific about the step rather than the task: is it that the reading is too long to hold, that the terminology will not resolve, that the ideas are there but come out in the wrong order, that the first sentence will not come, or that the whole thing is too big to start? They write it down. Then, and only then, they decide what would help, and check whether the help they are considering addresses the step they named or a different one. If a student cannot name the step, that is the finding, and it is worth taking to a tutor or a writing adviser rather than to a tool. Students keep the description; the same barrier usually recurs and they will stop rediscovering it. This is the student’s working document. Nobody else needs to see it, and the student does not need to explain to anyone why they made it.

before: Choosing an interview extract and a central evaluative question — in the source, what scientific, educational, and/or humanistic value the extract has — students give the extract to the chatbot in two separate threads, one carrying rich context about the interview and its background and one with little, then ask the same question in both. Comparing the two conversations for completeness, quality of reasoning, and moral consistency shows how much the framing did, and the discussion that follows draws out what this means for framing questions carefully and for bringing their own moral judgment to AI answers. The worked example used an OER oral history extract from the HumBox repository, an interview with Germinal Luis, a child refugee of the Spanish Civil War and World War II; the contributor ran it as a non-scientific experiment with ChatGPT-3 in January to February 2023, and current models may answer differently.

before: Students identify a discussion area relevant to the module, ask an AI tool of their choosing for a 300-word abstract on it, and place that abstract at the start of their essay, where it becomes the object their argument works on. They analyze it for what is accurate, what is inaccurate, and what needs expanding, then develop their own argument in a coherent narrative that draws on key readings and critical theories. Used as an assessment on a Digital Society and Education module with Year 3 students, and trialed in the year of writing with outcomes not yet reported, the essay makes AI text an object of analysis, so that the critical reasoning on display is legitimated by academic knowledge rather than by the fluency of the abstract.

before: The opening move is a question put to ChatGPT: “Can you be a debate partner and explain the rules?” With the rules on the table students name the topic, choose sides or let the chatbot assign them, set a time limit, and debate back and forth; less confident speakers can do this as a small group debating together against ChatGPT rather than alone. The practice round comes first, and peers come after. Because the contributor’s students had found debating useful while some lacked confidence in public speaking, rehearsing against a partner that will argue any position lets students examine every side of an issue and build the confidence and skill to hold it in front of people.

before: About 200 words on a stimulus is what each student asks the chatbot for — “What do you consider to be limitations of ChatGPT?” is the example — using ChatGPT or Perplexity, and the text that comes back is theirs to judge independently against a pro forma covering quality of English, quality of references, correct referencing style, and quality of argument. Groups of five then compare their texts and their pro forma reflections, and each group takes one of several routes from there: reaching consensus on the best text, ranking the texts, writing a better collaborative piece, or giving a joint presentation on their process and outcomes. Leaving the ending open keeps the discussion live, and the sequence develops referencing, summarizing, and group work alongside the critical thinking that judging an AI text requires.

before: Some claims cannot be settled by fact-checking, and predictions are the clearest case. Students generate a prediction, ideally one the instructor has specified in detail and vetted beforehand — the source’s samples concern cognitive microchips and the job market, a five-meter sea-level rise, and Social Security shortfalls — and evaluate what comes back for completeness, likelihood, and veracity, drawing on prior knowledge rather than on a source that could confirm or refute it. ChatGPT or another LLM will do; the sample prompts in the UCF FCTL guide were vetted with free ChatGPT 3.5 in mid-2023. The students’ evaluation of the prediction is what the use-case idea produces, and it puts reasoning and prior learning to work precisely where verification is not available.

before: Setting factual accuracy deliberately aside, students have ChatGPT or another LLM produce an argument or a syllogism — the source’s samples are a 250-word argument on no-fault insurance and a syllogism on turkeys as the national bird — and then examine only its structure: whether the conclusion follows, whether the evidence offered is necessary and sufficient, and what unstated warrant is holding it together. Those questions are answered in a written evaluation. The sample prompts come from the UCF FCTL guide and were vetted with free ChatGPT 3.5 in mid-2023. Ignoring whether the claims are true isolates validity as its own question, so an argument assembled from accurate parts can still be found unsound.

before: Coursework written by ChatGPT — or Copilot, or Bard — from prompts matching the real coursework arrives in a seminar or workshop, and students assess and mark it against the pre-identified marking criteria, looking in particular for missing technical language, critical review that stays shallow, and scholarly sources that turn out not to be genuine. The marking opens into discussion of how AI tools work, what they can do, how they might be used creatively, and where to draw the line, and it is paired with carefully constructed formative feedback. Inspired by reporting that ChatGPT fabricates references and used in an HE6 module, marking a machine’s work against the standard their own is held to brings its limitations, bias, and ethical concerns into view from the inside.

before: Working from the parameters of your own assessment, you enter them into ChatGPT and ask it to act as a client in your discipline writing a real-world brief; the example asked for a marketing campaign brief with budget, timescale, and market reach and got back a 6-month, $100,000 US campaign for smart thermostats, where a previous run had pitched eco-friendly water bottles. Once reviewed, that brief becomes the assessment task itself, with students producing materials in response to it. A variant has each student enter the parameters, so every scenario differs — the contributor notes how much variety regenerated briefs carry, which raises the question of comparable difficulty across them. The AI supplies the scenario; the marking criteria are not specified and remain yours. The appeal is authentic, varied tasks, which the contributor argues reduce copying while increasing inclusivity and applicability.

before: The rubric comes first and it is negotiated: participants and facilitators settle it together at the start, with iRubric suggested for the purpose. With the writing done, they ask ChatGPT for DALL·E 2 prompts that will generate an image to accompany it — the source’s examples are “Dragon in a fantastic world, dark background,” captioned as for a high-level output with something that can be improved, and “eagle flying in a clear blue mountain sky with open wings,” captioned as for a high-level output that does not need any change. Final feedback carries all three parts: the text, the prompt as a description of the image, and the image. An open plenary on the outputs and on how well the strategy worked closes it, the aim being discussion that goes deeper while asking less emotionally.

before: Students freewrite answers to a set of biographical questions — the setting of a favorite childhood memory, their talents, how they unwind, favorite food, how they dress, where they vacation — while deliberately not giving their identity away directly, then hand those answers to GPT-3 and ask it to infer aspects of their social identity. The reflection asks which information “exposed” their identities and why, and what might have “misled” the model; they go on to propose questions that would improve or impair its guesses and explain how the output would change. Running alongside literary texts on race and gender performance, the survey ends in discussion of the ethical implications for societal understandings of identity. Because personal information goes into the tool, privacy guidance is a live consideration.

Running the same critical attention in both directions is the design, since the model’s output is something they audit and the model is also an instrument they turn back on their own prose.

before: When no tutor is present to nudge the conversation along, the nudges can come from elsewhere: students enter a case study presented in class into ChatGPT and ask it for a list of topics the discussion should consider — ethics, boundaries, relationships, techniques — then use that list to guide the discussion their group actually has. The AI supplies the agenda, not the analysis, which stays with the students. Repeated across case study discussion workshops built on real-world cases, the list gradually becomes unnecessary as the key topics get internalized. For counseling students in the early, formative stages, that is what the nudge list is for: learning which considerations belong in a case discussion by having them named until students name them themselves.

before: Reading comes before writing here: students work through the interactive essay Mishkin made with GPT-3 and discuss how its author describes writing with the model — what it means to “drown in the power of suggestion,” and what it means for a story to take “the shape of the model.” With those phrases in hand they create a short narrative of their own using generative AI, then reflect on the practical affordances and the ethics of reading and writing text that is part human and part machine. Positioned as part of an introduction to an AI literacy module, the sequence moves them from consuming a hybrid text to producing one, so that thinking critically about generative text is tested against their own writing rather than only applied to someone else’s.

before: Against their own ethics on privacy, surveillance, authorship and IP, and bias and hallucination, students annotate a GenAI platform’s privacy policy or terms, working from a set of guiding questions: what data is collected, how it is stored and secured, who has access, whether users are informed, why the data is collected, whether consent is obtained, and whether users can control collection. A selection of clauses is then remediated — rewritten to match the ethics students have just articulated. Asking the platform itself to revise those same clauses produces a second version to set beside theirs, and the comparison is where bias becomes examinable. Gillo presents the work as developing critical analysis skills for safe and secure online behavior by prompting reflection on the data and privacy a user surrenders.

before: As a warm-up that calls for no materials and no AI tool, students finish two sentences: “When AI is working for us, it is like…” and “When AI is working against us, it is like…” An example metaphor may be put on the table first — the contributor’s mother’s, which the contributor offers for use with attribution, compares AI to fast food, quick and tasty but not healthy, though occasionally it saves us — which gives them a register to answer or resist. The metaphors then go into discussion, where the point is less whether an analogy holds than what it exposes, since the comparisons people reach for carry assumptions about dependence, convenience, and cost. Lightly at first and then more deeply, the exercise turns figures of speech into a way of talking about AI’s impacts.

before: Twelve days, twelve tools, one blog post a day: each post introduces a different AI tool with tips for educational use, and your part is a twenty-minute task with that day’s tool — writing a prompt, summarizing text, creating a video — followed by reflection questions that look critically at what using it in a classroom would involve. Built as a WordPress blog, the 12DoAI site ran as a live online program and stays open, so the twelve days can be worked through asynchronously, or the model can be adapted for another institution under the site’s own Creative Commons license, which permits noncommercial adaptation with attribution and share-alike. Twenty minutes a day is the whole commitment, and what it buys is confidence with tools you have not set up before, together with the habit of questioning them.

Prompting is demonstrated with Stable Diffusion and practiced until you arrive at techniques of your own, prompt engineering itself being held up for criticism along the way. The summative task moves outward: you use a GenAI tool of your choosing with your own students in an activity that promotes critical AI literacy, such as having them question the sources and facts in AI output. Running in Spanish for 1 ECTS, the course grounds GenAI theoretically and practically at once.

before: Two game-like, paper-based activities carry this, and neither needs a computer. In the first students add probability weightings to a network of word-type nodes until the chain generates grammatical phrases; in the second they build a chain out of an existing text extract, drawing a [Start] box linked to the first word and then, for each “current word,” counting its occurrences and drawing weighted arrows to the words that follow, closing with a [Stop] box after the last word. Running the finished chain generates text probabilistically, and students can see exactly why it produced what it did, because they drew every weight themselves. The discussion afterward asks what these word-to-word preferences reveal about how language models work and what they imply for linguistics.

before: Students in a communications or media course play a classroom version of Turing’s imitation game in groups of three to six. After a stretch of free questioning, the identities are revealed, and each group examines the exchange for the cues that separated person from machine, such as verbosity, strained slang, over-precise answers, and tone. The form is linked from the learning management system, and use that was not disclosed and later comes to light earns a zero for that task. The instructor then reads the accumulated forms as documents, coding students’ stated reasons to see where AI is being used to check work, for immediate help with procedures, under time pressure, or because of difficulty with the material. In the source’s general chemistry and honors citizen-science courses, most students reported high levels of use, and many pasted assignment questions directly into the tool. The author presents these patterns as a basis for revisiting assignment design and for discussing plagiarism, citation, and intellectual property with students.

before: A researcher with de-identified quantitative and qualitative data uses a general-purpose chatbot with data-analysis features as an assistant while keeping their own analysis as the reference. For the quantitative strand, the researcher shares a codebook, asks for suggested analyses, descriptive tables, and inferential tests, and uses their own statistical judgment to reject suggestions that do not fit the data. before: Qualitative researchers planning or reporting a study work through TROUT-AI, a set of yes-or-no questions grouped under five themes: the research team, participant interaction, study design, data practices, and data analysis. The questions ask, for example, whether an AI system acted in a researcher role and what AI training the team has, whether participants interacted with or were told about AI, how AI bore on sampling, saturation, participant checking, and ethics review, where data were stored and whether AI created data or interview protocols, and whether AI took part in coding and how coding was audited. before: Near the end of a first-semester introductory engineering or computing course, students receive a short program in a language they have not studied and, without discussing it, researching it, or using AI, add comments to the code and explain in plain English what they think it does. before: This participatory workshop for journalism students builds skill in recognizing automated social media accounts in political disinformation. In the first phase the instructor explains political communication online and the manipulation of the electoral public sphere, then gives a pretest in which students judge ten Twitter accounts as automated or not. In the second phase the class sees the pretest results, the instructor formalizes the intuitive knowledge students already showed and teaches the metadata features that mark bots, students try detection tools on the accounts they judged, and they take a comparable self-assessment test with items isolating single profile features in screenshots, plus open comments on how they identified accounts. In the third phase, results are presented collectively, and the class debates reporting mechanisms, publicizing these techniques, and cases where user action led to suspensions. With 55 students, the authors report average scores on the account identification questions of 6 out of 10 before the training and 5.7 out of 10 after it, while their abstract describes a slight increase in identification ability and a more conscious process of identification.

before: In a three-hour session midway through a postgraduate research-writing module, each of six participants first writes a project name and a 200-word abstract on their own researched topic without AI. before: Staff in a business school’s operations office who want to know which of their recurring tasks an agent could take on start by listing five recurring tasks with the hours each takes per week and asking a conversational model to sort them into fully, partly, or not automatable and to estimate the weekly time saved. before: Groups producing a short educational podcast in English for other learners rehearse their scripts before recording the final episode. Each speaker reads their section into a dictation-style speech-recognition tool and saves both the recording and the text it produces, so the script and the recognized text can be compared word by word. Every mismatch is treated as a question rather than a verdict: a partner listens to the saved rehearsal at that point and decides whether the word was unclear, whether the tool misheard speech that a listener understands without trouble, or whether the script itself is hard to say, for example a run of consonants or an ambiguous abbreviation. Students keep a log of these decisions and look for patterns, including whether the tool stumbles more on some group members’ accents than others, which the class can consider as a possible property of the recognizer and the speech it was trained on rather than a fault in the speakers. Speakers then rework the passages they judged unclear by practicing, re-recording, or rewriting the line, and listen to the second take with the same partner. The project log the course already keeps records the rehearsal texts, the mismatch decisions, and the changes made, and the finished episode credits any tool used in its production.

What is submitted is the description, the test cases, the table of alternatives with results, the adopted code with the student’s comments, and the log.

before: A first-year seminar opens with a debate about what intelligence is, and the questions it raises are written down for later. before: Library staff preparing a retrieval assistant for the library’s own service documents, such as loan policies, room-booking rules, and interlibrary-loan procedures written by staff, begin by assembling a fixed set of questions patrons actually ask, drawn from desk logs with identifying details removed, and noting for each the passage that answers it. A generative assistant then breaks each document into short, self-contained topical chunks that name their subject. Staff read every chunk against its source paragraph and correct merged facts, dropped conditions, and wording the source does not contain. Both versions, the raw documents and the checked chunks, are indexed, and the question set is run against each. For every answer, staff open the passages the assistant cites and code what went wrong, if anything, using the seven failure points from an engineering study of deployed retrieval systems: the answer was never in the documents, the right passage ranked too low, it was retrieved but left out of the answer’s context, it was present but not extracted, the format was wrong, the answer was too general or too specific, or it was incomplete. The team compares the two failure profiles, decides which documents need rewriting rather than re-chunking, and repeats the run after changes, keeping each coded log as a record of how the assistant behaved on the library’s own material before it is offered to anyone.

before: In a formative undergraduate pharmacology task, the instructor indexes a small source set in a document-grounded assistant: the instructor’s own mechanism notes, openly licensed treatment guideline summaries, and public-domain product labeling where it is available. Students put an instructor-written case question to the assistant, such as whether a given anticoagulant suits an older adult with reduced kidney function, and save the answer with the passages it cites. They pick out the claims that bear on safety and ask two questions of each: whether the cited passage actually says what the answer says, and whether the passage comes from the kind of source the claim needs, with mechanism claims drawn from the course notes, product safety from labeling, and treatment choice from guidelines. A correct-sounding claim cited to the wrong kind of source is logged as a retrieval error, separate from a claim the passage does not support. Students then set the assistant’s answer aside and work out the mechanism on their own, tracing how the drug’s target leads to its intended effect, to its risks, and to what needs monitoring, and testing that reasoning against the patient’s details. They revise the answer and add a short correction note naming what changed and which source or case detail justified it. The class compares logs to see whether retrieval errors cluster around particular questions or source types, a pattern the instructor can use to adjust the packet.

before: A research trainee reads each paper for a short review closely, annotates it with questions and first interpretations, and writes a synthesis across the set before consulting any AI tool; the set is drawn from openly licensed articles. Only then does the trainee give an assistant the full text of all the papers directly in a single request, without building an index or a retrieval step, together with the synthesis, and ask it to identify omissions and misrepresentations. Because a study of long inputs reports that models use material placed in the middle less reliably than material at the start or end, the trainee runs the same request a second time with the papers in a different order, moving the paper the trainee considers most important from first position to the middle of the set. Every gap or misreading the assistant flags in either run is checked against the original text and marked as confirmed, already addressed, or not supported by the paper. The trainee then compares the two critiques: which flags appear in only one run, and whether those concern papers that sat in the middle. A short note records which confirmed gaps led to revisions and what the comparison suggests about relying on a single critique of a long input. The synthesis remains the trainee’s own work throughout; the assistant’s role is to point at places worth rereading, and no paper is cited that the trainee has not read.

before: Students choose a well-known quotation attributed to a writer or public figure whose works are in the public domain, and record whom it is usually credited to and where they have seen it. They then trace it through three channels. The top results of an ordinary web search give one answer. A document-grounded assistant, into which the librarian has indexed the attributed author’s collected works from public-domain digital editions, gives another: students ask it where the words appear and save the passages it returns with their references. Because this kind of retrieval matches meaning rather than exact wording, it can return a passage that resembles the quotation in idea without containing it, so students check every returned passage with an exact-phrase search of the same text files and classify it as a verbatim match, a close paraphrase, a related idea, or nothing that supports the attribution. A passage the assistant presents as the source is never accepted on its word. Where nothing matches, students treat the absence as a finding to be tested rather than proof, searching a few distinctive words and checking letters or speeches the edition may not include. They finish with a verified or corrected attribution and a short account of what the search results, the assistant, and the primary text each said, including any passage the assistant offered that did not hold up.

before: In a short research-integrity workshop, researchers bring a small table of their own nonsensitive data and a description of the figure they intend to make from it. Each participant first asks a code-generation assistant for plotting code, reads it until they can vouch for every line, runs it, and saves the resulting figure with the code and the data source. Then, as a test rather than a production step, they give an image generator the same values and the same description and ask it to draw the figure. The two figures are laid side by side, and the generated one is audited mark by mark: values that do not match the table, axis ranges and tick labels that were changed or invented, legend entries for series that do not exist, error bars that were never supplied, and lettering that reads plausibly but says nothing. Participants tally what they find and share examples. Discussion links the tally to publisher policies that treat generated or manipulated images in papers as misconduct, and to why a figure that can be regenerated from code and data can be disclosed and checked in a way a picture cannot. Each participant leaves with the reproducible figure, its code, and a disclosure statement for the delegated coding task, while the generated chart is labeled and kept only as a workshop specimen.

before: In a business ethics unit on technology, students finish the assigned readings and, before any AI use, draft their own responses to a pair of workplace privacy questions. They then put the same questions to the institution’s licensed AI assistant, which they reach through campus sign-in under the institution’s agreement rather than through a personal consumer account, cite the response, and judge how well it answered and what grade it would earn. The second half of the assignment turns the unit’s questions on the tool itself. Using the institution’s published description of its AI service, and the terms of the agreement where they are public, students work out what happened to what they just typed: whether it is retained and for how long, whether it may be used to train models, which institutional roles can see logs, and what a consumer version of a similar tool would have done differently. They evaluate that arrangement with the same ethical frameworks they applied in their written answers, and say whether their own answer to the privacy questions changes now that they are, in effect, the employees whose inputs are governed by an employer’s contract. Answers, chatbot outputs, and evaluations are shared with the course, and discussion extends to what students would require of a vendor in their intended careers.

before: Preservice and in-service special educators practice drafting individualized education program goals from fictional, instructor-written student scenarios, with a question their future practice will raise: how much of a student’s information does a goal-writing tool actually need? For the first scenario each participant writes a goal unaided. For the second, they fill in a published structured goal template in two versions and submit each to the institution’s privately hosted AI service, which the program has approved and which does not retain prompts. The full version supplies every field, including the scenario’s invented name and disability identification; the minimized version replaces the name with a placeholder, omits the disability category, and keeps only the present level of performance, goal area, condition, behavior, criterion, and time frame. Participants rate all three goals, the unaided one and both generated ones, on six items of a published goal-rating instrument (whether the targeted behavior can be seen and counted, serves the student’s daily functioning, carries over to new settings, and can be taught by different team members across the day) and compare ratings with a partner. A short reflection names which fields could be left out without weakening the goal, which seemed to matter, and which they would never enter into any tool, approved or not, for a real student. The instructor gathers the field-by-field findings across the class and shares the pattern.

before: Students assemble a small corpus of handwritten letters from a public-domain digitized collection, saving each page image with a file name that carries the date and writer. Before any machine processing, each student reads and transcribes one page by hand, and that transcription becomes the reference for the page. The instructor or the students then send every page image to an image-reading model with a fixed transcription instruction and keep the raw output. As in the archival study the operation comes from, they compute character and word error rates on the hand-transcribed pages, run a second correction pass on a few pages, and measure whether it helped. The corpus is loaded into a web-based counting environment twice, once as raw machine text and once with the sample pages corrected, and students work through guided questions comparing the two: which frequent words change rank, which words that seem distinctive of a writer turn out to be misreadings, how spelling variants and abbreviations were silently modernized, and what a keyword-in-context search misses when one name is transcribed three different ways. Each claim students make about a writer’s vocabulary is checked against the page image of at least one occurrence. The products are the error-rate table, the paired frequency tables, and a short account of which findings survive correction.

before: Students analyzing financial statements work from an annual report the instructor has built as a PDF for a fictional company and laid out the way real reports are: income statement and balance sheet on different pages, a table continued across a page break, figures in thousands in one table and millions in another, a restated prior year in a footnote, and a chart that repeats some numbers. Each student first locates the needed figures, works out the three-part DuPont breakdown of return on equity, with its margin, turnover, and leverage components, and writes an interpretation. They then give the same PDF to a document-reading model with an instruction to extract each input with its page and table, show every step of the calculation, and state its assumptions, such as whether average or year-end equity was used. Students reconcile the two analyses figure by figure. Each difference is traced to the page and classified as a misread layout, an unconverted unit, a missed restatement, a different but defensible assumption, or an error of their own. A 300-word reflection compares the two analyses and states which conclusions about the company hold under both. Because the report is fictional and instructor-written, an answer key exists, and the layout features can be varied from one term to the next.

before: Each student chooses a documented photographic hoax from the nineteenth or early twentieth century whose images are in the public domain, such as the spirit photographs exposed in court in the 1860s, and researches how it was made and how it was exposed. They then test an image-reading model as a would-be verifier. In the first run the photograph goes in cropped of any caption or label, with a request to describe what is shown and say whether there are signs of manipulation. In the second, the same image goes in with its catalog caption. Students go through both responses one statement at a time and mark each as visible in the image, not visible, or supplied from elsewhere, paying particular attention to objects, attributes, and relations the model describes that are not there, and to claims about the photographer or technique that appear only once the caption is given. A short in-class presentation compares the model’s two accounts with the documented history of the hoax. Discussion follows on what was hardest to check, whether a model that recognizes a famous image is seeing it or remembering it, how this compares with earlier manipulation and its exposure, and whether and by whom image-reading tools should be relied on for verification.

before: Students receive, or generate for the occasion, a short biography of a well-documented figure in their institution’s history, written by a generative search engine with citations to web pages. Choosing someone with local records, such as archives, yearbooks, or news coverage, means the checking can be finished. Students first work through the biography with lateral reading in the SIFT pattern, stopping on each claim, investigating, finding better coverage, and tracing it to its origin, and they correct the errors they find. A second pass turns to the cited pages themselves. A recent audit of generative search engines, by its authors’ account, found that a meaningful share of cited pages showed signs of being machine-written, so students examine each cited page’s provenance by hand: whether an author or organization is named and can be found elsewhere, whether the page reports anything firsthand or only restates other pages, whether its dates and details agree with the archival record, and what the page seems designed to get readers to do. They do not run detection software, and they record a page as unestablished rather than machine-written when its origin cannot be determined. The product is a corrected biography with a source table that marks each cited page as reliable, secondary, or unestablished, and notes which errors in the biography trace to which pages.

before: An instructor in a religious studies course chooses a short narrative scene from a public-domain translation of a sacred text and, before class, generates two brief clips of it with a text-to-video tool: one from a deliberately general prompt that only names the scene, and one from a prompt that restates the passage’s own details. Students first read the passage closely and list what it actually specifies about setting, figures, objects, gestures, and sequence. They then watch each clip at full speed and afterward step through it, logging every visible element as grounded in the passage, borrowed from later artistic tradition, historically out of place, or without any basis the class can find. Because the medium moves, the log also captures what happens between frames: a vessel that appears and vanishes, a figure whose clothing changes from one moment to the next, an inscription that dissolves into unreadable marks, actions shown in an order the text does not give. before: A first-year seminar opens with a debate about what intelligence is, and the questions the debate raises are written down for later. A share of the photographs is held back, and the group records how often the trained model labels them correctly. Groups then take a second set of photographs designed to probe the model: the same objects on an unfamiliar background, in poor light, partly hidden, or replaced by look-alikes. These results are set beside the held-out accuracy, and each group writes what the pattern of errors suggests the model learned, which may turn out to be backgrounds or colors rather than materials. The debate is then rerun with each position required to cite a specific observation from the class’s models, and the original questions are revisited, along with how far one classifier can stand for other kinds of AI the students use, such as chat assistants or recommendation systems. The seminar closes with advice to developers that names a learning need or concern rather than novelty, and with a statement of what the classifier’s accuracy cannot establish, such as whether it has any concept of recycling.

before: Two game-like, paper-based activities carry this, and neither needs a computer. In the first you add probability weightings to a network of word-type nodes until the chain generates grammatical phrases; in the second you build a chain out of an existing text extract, drawing a [Start] box linked to the first word and then, for each “current word,” counting its occurrences and drawing weighted arrows to the words that follow, closing with a [Stop] box after the last word. Running the finished chain generates text probabilistically, and you can see exactly why it produced what it did, because you drew every weight yourself. The discussion afterward asks what these word-to-word preferences reveal about how language models work and what they imply for linguistics.
